summary: OpenAI describes training GPT-Red, an internal automated red-teaming model trained via self-play reinforcement learning, and its use in adversarially training GPT-5.6 to be more robust against prompt injection attacks.

mechanisms.reason: The lab states it dedicated an unprecedented amount of compute purely to training the red-teaming model at the scale of its largest post-training runs.
mechanisms.quote: We trained GPT‑Red at the compute scale of some of our largest post-training runs at OpenAI—an unprecedented amount of compute dedicated purely for improving safety.

practices.reason: GPT-5.6 Sol shows a quantified, stated reduction in prompt-injection failures relevant to teams building tool-using agents.
practices.quote: GPT‑5.6 Sol is our most robust model to prompt injections to date, achieving 6x fewer failures on our hardest direct prompt injection benchmark compared to our best production model from just four months earlier.

practices.reason: The self-play red-teaming methodology and its measured attack success rates against real agentic systems offer a transferable framework for evaluating prompt-injection robustness, though the model itself is kept internal-only.
practices.quote: GPT‑Red achieves significantly higher attack success rates, finding success on 84% of scenarios compared to 13% for humans.

practices.reason: The disclosed attack case studies (vending machine agent, Codex CLI agent data exfiltration) describe concrete third-party integration paths that need hardening and monitoring against prompt injection.
practices.quote: GPT‑Red deployed its attack against the production agent, achieving all three of its malicious objectives: Change the price of an expensive in-stock item to the minimum allowed price of $0.50; Order a new $100+ item and offer it for $0.50; and Cancel another customer’s order.
